terms.definition: The division that produces gametes: one round of DNA replication followed by two cell divisions, so that a diploid cell gives rise to haploid products. Its first division separates the members of each homologous pair from each other and its second separates sister chromatids, and it happens only in the germ line. A somatic tissue such as the colonic crypt never performs it.

The two versions of one chromosome that a person carries, one inherited from each parent. They are very similar in DNA sequence without being identical. The two are partners rather than copies of each other, and that distinction carries most of this lesson: partners are separated at the first meiotic division, copies at the second.

One of the strands of a chromosome that has been replicated. A chromosome that has just been copied consists of two chromatids joined at the centromere and still counts as one chromosome, so a cell can hold 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids at the same time. Keeping the two counts apart is the commonest difficulty in this material.

The two identical chromatids produced when one chromosome is replicated, joined at the centromere. Because one was copied from the other they carry the same DNA sequence, which is what distinguishes them from the two homologs of a pair. An ordinary mitotic division separates sister chromatids; meiosis separates them only at its second division.

The constricted region of a chromosome at which its sister chromatids are joined and at which the spindle takes hold to move it. In this lesson the centromere also carries information: a reciprocal exchange between homologs swaps the material beyond the point of exchange, so each chromatid keeps its own centromere, and the parental origin of a centromere is therefore what independent assortment sorts and what a marker can be read back from.

The structure formed when a replicated chromosome pairs with its replicated homolog during meiosis. A bivalent contains four chromatids: two sister chromatids from each of the two homologs. Some texts call the same four-chromatid structure a tetrad; this lesson uses bivalent throughout.

Holding both members of every homologous pair. A diploid human cell carries 46 chromosomes as 23 pairs. Ploidy counts chromosomes and not copies of DNA, so a cell whose chromosomes have just been replicated is still diploid even though it then holds two DNA copies of each chromosome. Somatic cells are diploid and stay diploid through every division they make.

Holding one member of every homologous pair. A haploid human cell carries 23 chromosomes. Because ploidy counts chromosomes rather than DNA copies, a cell can be haploid and still hold two copies of each chromosome's DNA: that is exactly the state after the first meiotic division, and it is why a second division is needed before the cell is a gamete.

A haploid cell whose function is to fuse with another gamete. In humans the two kinds are the sperm cell and the egg cell. Gametes are the only cells meiosis produces, and producing them is the only job meiosis does.

The single diploid cell formed when two gametes fuse. Every cell of the resulting body descends from it by ordinary division, which is why a chromosome error present in the zygote is present everywhere while one arising later is confined to a patch.
The lineage of cells that leads to gametes. It is the only lineage in which meiosis occurs. Novelty is the germ line's product: new combinations of chromosomes are what it exists to generate.

Any cell of the body that is not on the path to becoming a gamete. Somatic cells divide mitotically, remain diploid, and never undergo meiosis. Every cell in a colonic crypt is somatic, which is why genetic novelty there is damage rather than product.

The apparatus of protein fibres a dividing cell builds to move its chromosomes. It has two ends, called poles, and pulls each chromosome toward one pole or the other. Because one spindle has two poles, one division yields two cells, and that limit is the reason meiosis needs two divisions to reach four products.

The stage of a cell division at which the spindle actually pulls and the chromosomes move apart. Meiosis has two of them: at anaphase I the homologs separate, and at anaphase II the sister chromatids separate.

The rule that which member of one homologous pair goes to a given pole at the first meiotic division is settled independently of every other pair. With 23 pairs it gives a binary choice repeated 23 times, so 2 to the 23, about 8.4 million, distinct patterns of parental origin across the 23 centromeres. That count is exact for what it counts and ignores crossing over entirely.

The process in which meiosis deliberately breaks its own DNA and repairs each break using the homolog as the template. Most breaks are repaired without any exchange of arms; where the repair does produce a reciprocal exchange, the outcome is crossing over. Where this lesson writes recombination without qualification it means this meiotic process; the bare word is broader in general use and covers other kinds of DNA exchange that this lesson does not treat.

The reciprocal exchange of segments between two homologs during meiosis, so that beyond the point of exchange the DNA of one homolog's chromatid runs continuously into what was the other's. It does two jobs at once: it makes new combinations within a chromosome, and it physically ties the pair together so that the first division has something to pull against.

One completed reciprocal exchange between homologs, and so one countable event of crossing over. Crossovers are counted per meiotic cell by staining for a protein that gathers at them: measured means are about 49 per cell in human males and about 69 in human females, roughly two and three per chromosome pair. A crossover is a single event, whereas crossing over is the process that produces it.

The physical connection between two homologs produced by a crossover, and the thing that holds the pair together until the first anaphase separates them. A bivalent with no chiasma has nothing holding it, which is why an absence of crossing over leads to chromosomes being missegregated. The plural is chiasmata.

The protein glue holding sister chromatids together, running along the chromatid arms and also through the centromere. It is one substance in two locations, released in two stages: the arm cohesion at the start of anaphase I, and the centromeric cohesion only at the second division. That staging fixes the order of the two separations, and because the swapped arms beyond a crossover are held by arm cohesion, cutting it is also what lets the chiasma give way. This lesson shortens the name to cohesion where the context is chromosomes; it is unrelated to the cell-to-cell adhesion PREM-BIO-007 treats.

A reductional division reduces the number of chromosomes per cell; an equational division does not. Meiosis I is reductional because it separates the two homologs of each pair, taking a cell from 46 chromosomes to 23. Meiosis II is equational because it separates sister chromatids, which lowers the chromatid count while leaving the chromosome count at 23. An ordinary mitotic division is equational in the same sense.

The failure of chromosomes to separate normally during a division, leaving one product with an extra copy and another with none. In meiosis it can happen at either division, and the two cases leave different signatures: a failure at the first division yields products carrying two different homologs, and a failure at the second yields a product carrying two copies of one homolog.

A description of one position on a chromosome, comparing the copies a cell holds there. If the copies read differently in DNA sequence, the cell is heterozygous at that position; if they read the same, it is homozygous. The words describe the comparison at that position and nothing more, saying nothing about a whole chromosome and nothing about any trait. This lesson uses them only at the centromere, where they distinguish two copies that are different homologs from two copies of one homolog.

An unbalanced chromosome number, in which certain chromosomes no longer come in pairs. A balanced number is euploid. Aneuploidy can arise from a meiotic non-disjunction before an individual exists, or from a mitotic error afterwards, and telling those apart is a question about when rather than about the chromosomes themselves.

Trisomy is a diploid genome that has gained one chromosome, written 2N+1; monosomy is one that has lost a chromosome, written 2N-1. A gamete carrying two copies of a chromosome gives a trisomy on fusing with a normal gamete, and one carrying none gives a monosomy. Both are whole-chromosome changes, as distinct from segmental changes in which only pieces of chromosomes are gained or lost.

The small cell discarded at each of the two asymmetric divisions of oogenesis. Half the genome is segregated into the polar bodies, which is why one meiosis in the female yields a single functional gamete instead of four. The source this lesson follows describes two polar bodies, one per division; accounts giving three exist and the lesson records that disagreement rather than settling it.

Oogenesis is the production of egg cells in the ovary; spermatogenesis is the production of sperm cells in the testis. Both run meiosis and they run it differently: spermatogenesis divides symmetrically to four functional gametes and continues throughout life, while oogenesis divides asymmetrically to one functional gamete, begins before birth, and arrests in the first division for decades.

A cell with the capacity to self-renew and to produce differentiated progeny. The definition is about capacity rather than continuous activity: some stem-cell populations are quiescent until activated, while others cycle actively. In this lesson the term names the 12 to 16 cells at the base of a colonic crypt whose divisions renew the lining, and every one of those divisions is somatic.

alignment.note: PREM-BIO-001 defines stem cell for this course and this lesson keeps that meaning without alteration: capacity to self-renew and to produce differentiated progeny, with capacity distinguished from continuous division. Nothing is narrowed or extended, and the definition is not converted into an activity-based one even though this lesson quotes a division interval for the crypt population. PREM-BIO-006 adopted the same sense earlier. What this lesson adds is only that these divisions are somatic and so never meiotic.
